summary: Human insulin is recombinant insulin identical to endogenous hormone, used for glycaemic control in type 1 and type 2 diabetes and in diabetic emergencies. Regular (soluble) insulin has rapid onset and short duration and can be given IV; NPH (isophane) is intermediate-acting. Dosing is fully individualised; the principal hazard is hypoglycaemia, and never substitute insulin products or change concentration without close monitoring.
indications: Treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus when oral agents are inadequate
Control of hyperglycaemia in diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar states (regular insulin IV)
Glycaemic control in pregnancy (gestational and pre-existing diabetes)

dosage.n: Titrate to glucose targets; regular insulin ~30 min pre-meal

dosage.d: Start ~10 U or 0.1-0.2 U/kg/day basal; titrate to fasting glucose
Regular insulin ~0.1 U/kg/h IV infusion (+/- initial bolus per protocol)
dosage.n: Only regular insulin IV; monitor glucose and potassium hourly

dosage.d: Supplemental regular insulin per glucose and correction factor
dosage.n: Avoid as sole therapy; basal coverage required

admin: Regular insulin: SC ~30 minutes before meals; may be given IV/IM in emergencies
NPH (isophane) is given SC only - never IV; gently resuspend before use
Rotate SC injection sites (abdomen, thigh, arm, buttock) to avoid lipodystrophy
Do NOT substitute one insulin product/concentration for another without supervision
Store unopened insulin refrigerated; in-use pens/vials may be kept at room temperature for a limited period - do not freeze
moa: Insulin binds the insulin receptor on muscle, fat and liver, promoting cellular glucose uptake (via GLUT4 translocation), glycogen and lipid synthesis, and protein anabolism while inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis and ketogenesis - lowering blood glucose.

relative: Conditions worsened by fluid/sodium retention or hypokalaemia (caution)

preg: Insulin is the treatment of choice for diabetes in pregnancy; it does not cross the placenta in clinically significant amounts. Requirements change across trimesters - monitor closely and adjust.
lact: Compatible with breastfeeding; insulin is a protein not absorbed orally by the infant. Lactation may increase the risk of maternal hypoglycaemia - adjust intake/dose.
renal: Insulin requirements often decrease in renal impairment because of reduced renal clearance of insulin; monitor glucose closely and reduce dose to avoid hypoglycaemia.
hepatic: Insulin requirements may fall with reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis; monitor and adjust dose.

major: Other glucose-lowering agents (sulfonylureas, etc.) - additive hypoglycaemia
Beta-blockers - may blunt warning signs of hypoglycaemia and alter recovery
moderate: Corticosteroids, thiazides, atypical antipsychotics, sympathomimetics - raise glucose, may need higher insulin dose
ACE inhibitors, fibrates, MAOIs, salicylates - may enhance glucose-lowering
Thiazolidinediones - fluid retention/heart failure risk when combined
interactions.food: Match insulin to carbohydrate intake and meal timing; missed meals risk hypoglycaemia.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol potentiates and prolongs hypoglycaemia and impairs awareness; avoid or use cautiously with food.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers blood glucose and HbA1c; can lower serum potassium.

rare: Worsening of diabetic retinopathy with rapid glucose improvement
emergency: Severe hypoglycaemia with loss of consciousness

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia
Serum potassium, especially with IV insulin/DKA
counsel: Recognise and treat hypoglycaemia early (sweating, tremor, hunger, confusion) - carry fast-acting glucose
Inject regular insulin about 30 minutes before meals and do not skip meals
Rotate injection sites and never share pens or needles
Do not change your insulin brand, type or strength without your doctor's advice
Tell your doctor about illness, alcohol, exercise changes or new medicines - your dose may need adjusting
pk: Short (regular IV minutes); action prolonged by SC absorption
Refrigerate unopened (2-8 C); in-use kept at room temp briefly; do not freeze
pearls: Only regular (soluble) insulin may be given intravenously - never NPH or mixtures IV
Insulin requirements fall in renal/hepatic impairment - reduce dose and monitor
Beta-blockers can mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia
Watch potassium - insulin drives K+ into cells (used to treat hyperkalaemia)
Never substitute insulin products or concentrations without close supervision
missed: Insulin timing is tied to meals - do not take a missed mealtime dose long afterwards. Check blood glucose, follow your sick-day/missed-dose plan, and contact your care team if unsure; never double the next dose.
overdose: Excess insulin causes hypoglycaemia which may be severe (seizures, coma). Treat mild cases with oral fast-acting carbohydrate; treat severe/unconscious cases with IV glucose (dextrose) or glucagon, then ongoing carbohydrate and glucose monitoring; watch for hypokalaemia.
